Bad
băd
adj. (evil, worthless, rotten; rendering Hebrew ra, Greek sapros, poneros, and kakos)
Middle English badde, of uncertain descent. The Authorized Version uses the word sparingly and almost always in a pair: good or bad.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

In Scripture bad nearly always stands beside good and marks a judgment between them. Laban and Bethuel “cannot speak unto thee bad or good” (Gen 24:50); Solomon asks for an understanding heart “that I may discern between good and bad” (1Ki 3:9); Jeremiah's figs are “very good” and “very naughty figs, which could not be eaten, they were so bad” (Jer 24:2). The net gathers of every kind, and the fishermen “gathered the good into vessels, but cast the bad away” (Mat 13:48); the wedding is furnished with guests “both bad and good” (Mat 22:10). And at the judgment seat every one receives “the things done in his body, according to that he hath done, whether it be good or bad” (2Co 5:10).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines bad as ill; not good; evil; vicious; wicked; unwholesome; unfortunate; a word of general application.

expand to see more

BAD, a. Ill; not good; evil; vicious; wicked; the opposite of good.

2. Unwholesome; as bad air.

3. Unfortunate; unprosperous; as a bad state of affairs.

4. Imperfect; not sound; as a bad debt.

Key Scripture

2Co 5:10 — "For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ; that every one may receive the things done in his body, according to that he hath done, whether it be good or bad."

Mat 13:48 — "Which, when it was full, they drew to shore, and sat down, and gathered the good into vessels, but cast the bad away."

1Ki 3:9 — "Give therefore thy servant an understanding heart to judge thy people, that I may discern between good and bad: for who is able to judge this thy so great a people?"

Mat 22:10 — "So those servants went out into the highways, and gathered together all as many as they found, both bad and good: and the wedding was furnished with guests."

Jer 24:2 — "One basket had very good figs, even like the figs that are first ripe: and the other basket had very naughty figs, which could not be eaten, they were so bad."

Modern Corruption

Good and bad is treated as a spectrum with everyone somewhere in the middle, and the net in Matthew 13 has only two piles.

expand to see more

Modern morality prefers a gradient: nobody is bad, some are less good, and everyone is somewhere on the line. The parable of the net ends with two piles on the shore and nothing between them. “So shall it be at the end of the world: the angels shall come forth, and sever the wicked from among the just.” The wedding hall in Matthew 22 was filled with bad and good together, and the king still walked the room and found the man without a garment. The gathering is indiscriminate; the sorting is not.

Second Corinthians 5:10 is addressed to Christians. Paul says “we must all appear,” and the reckoning is of things done in the body, good or bad. The doctrine of a judgment of works for the justified is not a threat to their justification — the same letter says they are new creatures and reconciled — but it is the reason Paul gives, in the very next verse, for persuading men: “Knowing therefore the terror of the Lord.” A gospel that has removed every consequence from the believer's conduct has removed the sentence Paul used to keep himself sober.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew ra (H7451), evil, bad, of poor quality; Greek sapros (G4550), rotten, worthless; poneros (G4190), evil; kakos (G2556), bad.

expand to see more

Hebrew ra (H7451) — evil, bad, worthless; Genesis 24:50, 31:24, 1 Kings 3:9, Jeremiah 24:2, Leviticus 27:10.

Greek sapros (G4550) — rotten, unfit; Matthew 13:48, the bad fish; Matthew 7:17, the corrupt tree.

Greek poneros (G4190) — evil, wicked; Matthew 22:10; and kakos (G2556), 2 Corinthians 5:10.

Usage

"“Cast the bad away” — two piles on the shore."

"“Whether it be good or bad” — the reckoning Paul kept before himself."

"“Discern between good and bad” — what Solomon asked for instead of riches."
